blog.why_developer_tooling_is_the_best_b: Why Developer Tooling Is the Best Bet in SaaS Right Now
blog.the_saas_landscape_has_shifted_five:
The SaaS landscape has shifted. Five years ago, the low-hanging
            fruit was in vertical software — practice management for dentists,
            scheduling for gyms, invoicing for freelancers. That fruit has
            been picked. The verticals are crowded, margins are thin, and
            differentiation is hard when every competitor is built on the
            same Stripe and Twilio stack.
blog.developer_tooling_is_different_when:
Developer tooling is different. When you build something that
            engineers use every day, you embed yourself into their workflow.
            Switching costs are real and organic — not engineered through
            data lock-in or artificial friction. A great CLI tool, a
            well-designed SDK, or a smarter CI step becomes part of how a
            team thinks about their work, not just something they pay for.
blog.the_best_developer_tools_share_a_co:
The best developer tools share a common trait: they make
            something that was previously annoying either disappear entirely
            or shrink to a single command. The annoyance does not have to be
            dramatic. It can be something as mundane as approving translation
            strings before a release, or copying environment variables
            between team members. Small pain, applied daily across a
            hundred-person engineering org, is a real product opportunity.
blog.for_the_past_two_years_the_most_int:
For the past two years, the most interesting developer tools have
            not been frameworks or libraries — they have been agentic systems
            that sit on top of your existing stack. The pattern is consistent:
            find a workflow that requires human judgment but follows a
            repeatable structure, then automate the judgment with a language
            model while keeping the human in the loop for edge cases.
blog.localization_is_a_perfect_example_t:
Localization is a perfect example. The old workflow: developer
            wraps strings in i18n calls, sends a PR for review, a localization
            manager exports a CSV, sends it to a translation agency, waits a
            week, imports the results, and merges. Every step has a human
            touching a file. The new workflow: a bot scans the PR, injects
            the i18n calls automatically, and translates everything with
            confidence scoring before the developer refreshes their browser.
            The human only intervenes when confidence is low.
blog.this_is_not_about_replacing_jobs_tr:
This is not about replacing jobs. Translators and localization
            managers still review, refine, and own the voice of the product
            in each market. What disappears is the mechanical coordination
            overhead — the CSV exports, the JIRA tickets, the Slack threads
            asking where the strings file is.
blog.what_makes_a_developer_tool_defensi: What Makes a Developer Tool Defensible
blog.the_tools_that_last_are_the_ones_th:
The tools that last are the ones that get smarter with use. A
            static linter is replaceable. A linter that learns your team's
            specific patterns, flags the edge cases your team keeps hitting,
            and integrates directly into your CI pipeline is not. Network
            effects compound at the team level rather than the user level,
            which means your churn dynamics are completely different from a
            consumer app.
blog.if_you_are_building_in_this_space_m:
If you are building in this space, my advice is to pick one
            workflow that engineers hate and make it invisible. Not better.
            Not easier. Invisible. That is the bar worth aiming for.
